chapter: Origins of jazz and the district
title: Red-light district music was not early jazz
summary: Brown rejects the writers' view that jazz came from the district; its barrelhouse, slow-drag music differed from his lively dance music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: What you're about to talk about is the music from the Red Light District, you said that wasn't really typical.

To me, no, that's completely out. That's wrong. But the majority of writers, they could... But that's the easiest way to write about it, see? That everything came from the district. That's right, but it isn't. So the music down there was entirely different.
What kind of music did they have in the district?

Barrel House and, as I call it, bump music and slow drag music. We never played no slow drags and things like that. What were the slow drags? Slow drag? It was a regular four-fourth piece and real slow with a lot of bumps. Would they be blues sometimes?

In the form of blues, yes. Now we couldn't play in that type of slow tempo. All our tempos were lively. And it was entirely different. And we couldn't... Anyway, it wasn't the same type of music that Tom brought up to Chicago. It was named jazz. And that's what everybody is in college as. That was what everyone is interested in, see? And while the story of the reflection of that part, you know what I mean, what they call it, the way Tom considers it, couldn't be classed as a music that was coming directly from there, see? Now Tom, the type of music we played down there, we could never get a job in any of the places down in the... the tenor line district and play. Because our music would be too fast, too lively.
